cover.headline: India's No. 2 card issuer is past the worst of its credit cycle and trades at 16x next year's earnings; the catch is that growth has stalled and fundamentals alone do not support the price
cover.lead: SBI Card has 2.26 crore cards in force (18.6% of India's) and 19.5% of card spends. Two years of heavy loan losses (gross credit cost 9.1% of receivables in FY25, 8.8% in FY26 on our basis) cut profit 20% and halved ROE to ~15%. Q1FY27 showed the turn: credit cost 6.5%, profit +20%, ROE 16.5%. But receivables grew only 3% and pre-provision profit fell 12%. The street values the stock on **P/E (18-22x FY28E EPS)**. We forecast EPS of ₹29.8 / ₹36.2 / ₹41.0 for FY27-29E and ROE of ~17%. Applying **21x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹38.6** (derived from its own credit-cycle-adjusted history, the post-FY24 growth regime and the sector's de-rating) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY.** Be clear about what that assumes: the market pays ~21x again for a 17% ROE business. Our intrinsic checks (justified P/B ₹468, residual income ₹452) sit below today's price. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The credit cycle has turned, and it drives FY27-28
arguments.p: Gross credit cost fell from 9.5% in Q1FY26 to 6.5% in Q1FY27; GNPA 2.04% and Stage 2 3.57% are post-COVID lows; entry into the first delinquency bucket is at a "decadal low" (management). At {{F.creditCost.0|pct}} of receivables in FY27E, profit grows {{F.patGrowth.0|pct}} even with flat pre-provision profit. Each 10bp of credit cost is ~1.4% of FY28E profit.

arguments.h: A franchise SBI built and keeps feeding
arguments.p: Nearly half of new cards come through SBI's branches (47% in Q1FY27), the cheapest and best-quality channel any Indian issuer has; co-brands (BPCL, Flipkart, Tata Neu, IndiGo, PhonePe) bring the rest. New accounts are back above 10 lakh a quarter (+17%). SBI also lends it ₹19,900 cr (45% of borrowings) and owns 68.6%.

arguments.h: But growth has stalled and income quality has slipped
arguments.p: Receivables grew 2% in FY26 and 3% in Q1; revolvers (the most profitable balances) fell to 22% of the book; spend growth comes from thin-margin corporate cards. NIM fell 28bp in Q1 to 10.8% and cost-to-income rose to 58.7%. We model receivables +{{F.aumGrowth.0|pct0}} / +{{F.aumGrowth.1|pct0}} / +{{F.aumGrowth.2|pct0}}: below the 22% CAGR of FY19-24 and dependent on the H2 pick-up management promised.

arguments.h: Valuation: cheap on its history, full on fundamentals
arguments.p: At ₹578 the stock trades at 19.4x FY27E and 16.0x FY28E EPS, the lowest forward multiple since listing; its credit-cycle-adjusted forward P/E has a 26.4x median since Apr-2024 and listed lenders trade 11% below their own medians. Our 21x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}. At a 13.1% cost of equity the price already implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} long-run ROE, above the 16-18% that management's 4-4.5% ROA target supports.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): whether the promised H2 receivables pick-up starts and credit cost holds near 6.5%.
Festive quarter (Q3FY27): spends, EMI conversion and acquisition costs; cost-to-income guided to peak in this quarter.

RBI: whether the lower risk weight on transactor balances (final for banks from 1-Apr-2027) is extended to NBFC card issuers; the final rule on NBFC revolving credit (draft of 6-Aug-2026 exempts card issuers).
Leadership: the MD & CEO's two-year SBI deputation runs to about Mar-2027; a renewal or successor decision is due before then.
Capital: CAR 25.6% against a 15% minimum; any change in payout (11-12% now) would show whether the surplus will be returned.

sections.title: A pure-play card issuer: it earns on every swipe, and more on the customers who do not pay in full

blocks.p: SBI Cards and Payment Services (SBI Card) issues credit cards and nothing else; it has no subsidiaries and one reportable segment. It is India's second-largest issuer, with 2.26 crore cards in force (an 18.6% share in June 2026) and 19.5% of national card spends. State Bank of India owns 68.6%. The company is regulated by the RBI as a non-deposit-taking NBFC, which matters: it cannot take deposits, so it funds itself with bank loans, commercial paper and bonds, and it is subject to NBFC capital rules (minimum capital 15% of risk-weighted assets).

A card issuer earns money in three ways. **Interest** from customers who do not pay their full bill (revolvers, who pay card interest rates well above a personal loan's) or who convert purchases into instalments (EMI). **Fees on spending**: every time a card is used, the merchant's bank pays the issuer an interchange fee on the bill (1.19% of spends on average for SBI Card in FY26), so spend volume matters even when the customer pays in full. **Other fees**: annual and joining fees, late-payment fees, cash-advance and foreign-exchange charges, and incentives from the card networks (Visa, Mastercard, RuPay). Against that it pays for funding (~6.5%), for rewards, marketing and processing (spend-linked costs that rise with every swipe) and for bad debts.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** a card issuer is part lender, part payments business. The payments half (interchange, fees) grows with spending and carries little credit risk; the lending half (revolve, EMI) earns the margin but carries the losses. SBI Card's mix has tilted towards payments: transactors (who pay in full) were 45% of receivables in Q1FY27 against 40% a year earlier, and corporate cards (no lending at all) supplied about half of FY26's 29% spend growth. That is safer, but it earns less per rupee of receivables.

sections.title: From a GE joint venture to a listed SBI subsidiary, through two credit cycles

blocks.p: SBI Card was set up in 1998 as a joint venture of State Bank of India and GE Capital. GE sold its 40% in December 2017 (SBI took 14%, Carlyle's CA Rover 26%); the company listed in March 2020, days before the Covid lockdown, as India's first pure-play listed card issuer. Carlyle sold down in 2021. The decade since 2016 shows two credit cycles (Covid in FY21, the unsecured-lending hangover in FY25-26), a burst of growth in between, and a string of regulatory changes that each moved the numbers.

sections.title: Credit cards in India: ~12 crore cards held by only ~5.5 crore people, and an industry stuck in the slow lane

blocks.p: India had about 118.6 million credit cards at Mar-2026 (110 million a year earlier) and ~121 million by June 2026; card spends grew ~12% to ₹23.6 lakh crore in FY26 (RBI data, per SBI Card). Penetration is still thin: management puts India's card customers at 52-55 million people, against ~350-400 million with a credit-bureau record and an SBI customer base of 53 crore. PwC projects ~210 million cards and ₹54 lakh crore of annual spends by FY30. The runway is real.

The last two years were slower. After unsecured-credit stress in FY24-25, issuers tightened underwriting; cards-in-force growth slipped to mid-single digits and "very few new customers are being brought into the fold" (MD, Q4FY26 call): most new cards go to people who already hold one. Spending kept growing, but more of it on corporate cards (thin margins) and on UPI-linked RuPay cards in smaller towns, and fewer customers revolve. Personal loans compete directly: "if he has an option of lower-priced personal loan, he will take a personal loan" (MD, Q1FY27 call), one reason SBI Card's revolver share fell from 24% to 22%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the industry will keep growing for a decade; penetration is too low for it not to. The question for SBI Card is share and quality of growth. It has held 18-19% of cards and gained spend share (to 19.5%), but the profitable part of the business (revolving balances) is under pressure from personal loans and from its own tighter underwriting. Regulation is, for once, tilting slightly in its favour (transactor relief, the NBFC revolving draft).

sections.kicker: Does the tailwind reach SBI Card?
sections.title: Tailwind test: which trends actually help SBI Card's returns?

blocks.p: An industry trend only matters to a shareholder if the company turns it into profit. We score each one.

verdicts: Gross credit cost 9.5% (Q1FY26) → 6.5% (Q1FY27); GNPA 3.07% → 2.04%; Stage 2 at a post-COVID low; first-bucket entry rates at a "decadal low".
The single biggest driver of FY27-28 profit in our model.
Industry cards +8% in FY26, spends +12%; SBI Card spends +29%, new accounts +17% in Q1.
Spends turn into fees, but receivables (where the margin is) grew only 2-3%.
Online is 63% of retail spends; Flipkart, Tata Neu, IndiGo, PhonePe, BPCL (5 million cards) co-brands.
Brings engaged, credit-tested customers at a lower acquisition cost than open-market sourcing.
UPI spends +13% QoQ; 80% of UPI-active cards in Tier 2+ towns.
More transactions and activation, but thinner interchange; supports volume more than profit.
Corporate spends +125% YoY in Q1 to ~20% of spends.
Adds fee income with "comparatively thinner" margins (pass-back costs); lifted cost-to-income from 51.8% to 55.3%.
Cost of funds fell 82bp YoY to 6.4% in Q4FY26; 6.5% in Q1FY27.
Management now expects funding costs to drift up with market rates.
Personal loans and NBFC consumer finance
Cheaper personal loans and NBFC EMI loans take revolve and big-ticket EMI business.
A structural cap on the revolver share (22%) and on yields.
Transactor relief (if extended to NBFCs), NBFC revolving-credit draft exempts card issuers; but 125% risk weights stay and BPSP curbs hit corporate spends.
Net slightly positive from here; not in our base case.

blocks.title: Tailwind scorecard: the credit turn helps most; personal-loan competition pushes back
blocks.source: Company presentations and calls (Q4FY26, Q1FY27); annual report FY26; GAM Research

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the trend that matters most in FY27-28 (lower credit costs) is cyclical. The structural tailwinds (penetration, online spending, co-brands) show up mainly in spends and fee income, while the structural headwind (personal loans eating revolve) hits the highest-margin balances. That is why our ROE recovers to ~17%, not to the 22-26% SBI Card earned when revolvers were a quarter of the book and growth was 25%+.

sections.title: Cards are growing again; receivables are not, yet

blocks.p: SBI Card sources new customers through two channels. **Banca** (State Bank of India's branches and its YONO app) brought 47% of new accounts in Q1FY27 and 46% in FY26; it gives SBI Card customers whose banking history SBI already sees (salaried, government and PSU employees among them), which is the cheapest, lowest-risk sourcing any Indian issuer has. **Open market** (53%) means co-brand partners (BPCL, Flipkart, Tata Neu, IndiGo, PhonePe, Apollo, IRCTC and others) and direct sales. Management's target is 50-55% banca. New accounts fell from 52 lakh in FY23 to 36 lakh in FY26 as underwriting was tightened, and are now rising again: 10.2 lakh in Q1FY27 (+17%), with the industry's highest net card additions (4.84 lakh).

pair.title: New accounts: cut back after FY23, now rising again
Receivables per card are falling
pair.unit: Gross receivables ÷ cards in force at March (₹)

blocks.p: Why receivables stalled while cards grew: (1) tighter credit limits after the FY25 stress ("maybe we were slightly conservative", MD) — limits are now being raised again for eligible customers; (2) more customers paying in full: transactors rose from 40% to 45-46% of receivables; (3) revolvers shrank from 24% to 22% as some moved to cheaper personal loans; (4) the new accounts of FY26 were fewer and take a year or more to build balances. Management expects growth to pick up from H2FY27 (higher acquisition, festive season), but gave no number.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we assume receivables grow 8% in FY27E (Q1 already +2.4%; Q2FY26 alone added 5.7%) and 12-13% in FY28-29E as the larger FY27 card cohorts build balances and limits are raised. That is half the FY19-24 pace. Receivables fall from 13% of annual spends in FY26 to ~12% because spends (corporate, UPI) grow faster than lendable balances. Bull case: +11/15/16%; bear: +4/8/9%.

sections.title: Half the revenue comes from fees; we model them from spends, and the take rate is falling

blocks.p: Fees and other operating income were ₹9,999 cr in FY26, as large as interest income (₹9,901 cr). Interchange alone was ₹5,111 cr: 1.19% of ₹4.3 lakh cr of spends, down from ~1.4% in FY21-FY22 as lower-rate spending (corporate cards, UPI-RuPay) grew faster. Late and other fees (₹2,817 cr) fell 2% as fewer customers paid late, and membership fees (₹1,238 cr) grew 2%. We therefore build fees bottom-up from spends rather than as a flat share of receivables.

blocks.p: **The cost side moves with spends too.** Rewards (₹1,488 cr in FY26, +35%), card transaction charges (₹977 cr, +28%), fees and commission paid (₹1,213 cr, +92%, mainly pass-backs on corporate spends) and sales promotion (₹2,804 cr) together were ~66% of FY26 operating cost. That is why a spend boom does not lift profit one for one: management guides cost-to-income of 56-58% for FY27 (58.7% in Q1). Each 1bp of interchange take rate is worth ~1.25% of FY28E profit.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** fees grow ~9% in FY27E and ~11-12% a year after, a little faster than receivables, because spends grow 15%+. The risk is the take rate: we cut it 2-4bp a year; a faster shift to UPI-RuPay and corporate spends would cost more.

sections.title: NIM: high by lending standards, but drifting down as revolvers shrink

blocks.p: On our basis (all interest income ÷ average March receivables), the yield was {{fin.yieldOnAum.11|pct}} in FY26 and NIM {{fin.nim.11|pct}}; on the company's basis (cardholder interest only, monthly averages) yield was 16.5% and NIM 11.2%. Both are high because only ~55% of receivables earn interest, and those revolve or EMI balances earn far more than a bank loan. The direction is down: company yield fell from 17.6% (FY22) to 16.5% (FY26) and 16.0% in Q1FY27, and NIM fell 28bp QoQ to 10.8% in Q1, as revolvers fell to 22% and lower-yield EMI balances grew. Cost of funds helped in FY26 (6.7% vs 7.4%) but management now expects it to "trend higher in line with market rates".

Upside if limit increases and the festive season revive revolve; downside if personal loans keep taking revolvers.

sections.title: Credit costs: down from 9.5% to 6.5% in a year; the question is where they settle

blocks.p: A card book is unsecured and short: when a customer stops paying, there is no collateral, so SBI Card writes the balance off quickly (Stage 3 covers only 90-179 days past due) and books most of its loss as write-offs rather than as provisions. That is why "credit cost" here means gross write-offs plus the change in provisions, and why it is so much higher than at a secured lender: 6-9% of receivables a year, against interest and fee income of ~35%. In FY25 write-offs jumped 64% to ₹4,732 cr as stress in unsecured consumer credit across the industry came through; FY26 was almost as bad (₹4,926 cr). The cycle turned during FY26: gross credit cost fell from 9.5% (Q1FY26) to 7.7% (Q4FY26) and 6.5% in Q1FY27, GNPA from 3.07% to 2.04%, and Stage 2 (30-89 days overdue) to 3.57%, the lowest since Covid.

blocks.p: **Provisions and buffers.** Expected-credit-loss provisions were 3.1% of receivables in Jun-2026 (3.5% a year earlier) and covered 59.9% of Stage 3 loans. The annual model refresh in Q1FY27 used ₹180 cr of the ₹220 cr management overlay held at March; ₹65 cr was released as the portfolio mix improved, and ₹70 cr of overlay is still held against geopolitical risk. Q1's 6.5% therefore includes a small release; gross write-offs alone were 7.0% of average receivables. A card book turns over fast, so a new stress wave would reach profit within two or three quarters.

blocks.callout: **Our forecast:** gross credit cost of {{F.creditCost.0|pct}} / {{F.creditCost.1|pct}} / {{F.creditCost.2|pct}} for FY27-29E: Q1's run-rate for FY27 (management: "within the current range", "some more moderation"), then a little lower and edging up as the larger new-card cohorts season. That is below our 7.2% through-cycle level (the median of FY19 and FY23-FY26), so our profits are cyclically flattered and we adjust for it in the valuation. Each 10bp of credit cost is ~1.4% of FY28E profit; the bear case (7.4-7.6%) cuts FY28E EPS to ₹{{scen.bear.eps.1|n2}}.

sections.title: Funding: AAA-rated and backed by its parent, but priced like a non-bank

blocks.p: SBI Card cannot take deposits, so it borrows: ₹44,064 cr at Mar-2026 and ₹47,176 cr at Jun-2026, from bank lines (working-capital loans and term loans), commercial paper and bonds, including subordinated debt that counts as capital. It is rated AAA/Stable (long term) and A1+ (short term) by CRISIL and ICRA. The parent matters here too: State Bank of India had lent it ₹19,876 cr at Mar-2026, 45% of all borrowings, and earned ₹1,357 cr of its ₹3,072 cr finance cost in FY26 (related-party note, "at arm's length"). Card receivables are short (most are repaid within a month or two, EMIs within about a year), so funding is mostly short term too; the company reports positive cumulative asset-liability gaps in every bucket.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** with SBI behind it, SBI Card has never had a funding scare, and its cost of funds (6.5%) is low for a non-bank. But it has no low-cost current and savings deposits, so bank issuers fund the same card balances more cheaply. Its funding cost also reprices fast with market rates; management expects it to drift up, and we add 10-20bp in FY27-28E.

sections.title: Capital: 25.6% against a 15% minimum; the problem is too much equity, not too little

blocks.p: Capital adequacy was 25.6% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 20.3%) against RBI minimums of 15% and 10%. It fell to 20.5% at Mar-2024 after the RBI raised the risk weight on card receivables from 100% to 125% in Nov-2023 (the company estimated a ~4pp hit), and has rebuilt as profit was retained and the book stopped growing. Assets were 4.2x equity at Mar-2026 against 4.8x at Mar-2024. Asked why it paid a dividend in a weak year, the MD said: "We are underleveraged actually."

Two things could free more capital. (1) The RBI's credit-risk rules for banks cut the weight on transactor balances (customers who pay in full) from 125% to 100% from 1-Apr-2027; if the NBFC rules follow, ~40% of SBI Card's receivables would carry less capital (a press estimate put the release at ~450bp of capital ratio). We found no final NBFC version by 30-Sep-2026. (2) A higher payout: the company paid ₹2.50 a share for FY26 (11% of EPS). Our base case keeps a 12% payout, so equity compounds at ~15-16% against receivables growth of 8-13% and leverage keeps falling to {{fin.assetsToEquity.14|n2}}x assets to equity by FY29E. That alone holds ROE near 17%.

pair.title: Leverage falls in our model unless payout rises

blocks.callout: **Our view:** SBI Card does not need equity for years; it needs growth or a higher payout. At a 12% payout and ~17% ROE, equity grows ~15% a year. If receivables grow less than that, capital piles up and ROE drifts down. A higher payout would hold ROE up, but SBI, as the 69% owner, has given no sign of asking for one. DPS: ₹{{F.dps.0|n2}} / ₹{{F.dps.1|n2}} / ₹{{F.dps.2|n2}} in FY27-29E.

sections.title: From ROA to ROE: ~5% on receivables, levered ~3.3x, gives ~17%

blocks.p: A lender's return on equity is its return on assets times leverage. A card issuer's tree looks unlike any other lender's: huge income lines (interest plus fees ~35% of receivables), huge costs (operating cost ~17-18%, credit cost 6-9%), and a thin result that swings with credit cost. Because SBI Card runs low leverage (receivables ~3.6x equity), it needs a ~5% return on receivables to earn 17%.

blocks.callout: **What changes:** FY27E return on receivables recovers to {{F.roaAum.0|pct}} because credit cost falls ~2pp while pre-provision profit slips. After that, operating leverage helps a little (opex falls from {{F.opexPct.0|pct}} to {{F.opexPct.2|pct}} of receivables) but leverage keeps falling, so ROE peaks at {{F.roe.1|pct}} in FY28E. Management's medium-term ROA target of 4-4.5% (on total assets) is in line with our FY28-29E ({{F.roa.1|pct}}, {{F.roa.2|pct}}, the top of the range); it is not consistent with a return to the 22-26% ROEs of FY22-FY24 without much more leverage.

sections.title: From 25% ROE to 15% in two years; the way back runs through credit costs, not growth

blocks.p: SBI Card grew net profit from ₹284 cr in FY16 to a peak of ₹2,408 cr in FY24, about 31% a year, with returns on equity of 22-32% in most years. Then the model broke. Receivables growth fell from 25-30% a year (FY22-FY24) to 10% in FY25 and 2% in FY26, and loan losses rose to 9% of receivables as unsecured borrowers who had taken too much credit stopped paying. Profit fell 20% in FY25 to ₹1,916 cr and recovered only 13% in FY26 to ₹2,167 cr; ROE halved to under 15%. Q1FY27 is the first quarter that looks better: profit ₹664 cr (+20%) as credit costs fell to 6.5%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the FY27-29E profit recovery is mostly a credit-cost story. Pre-provision profit barely grew in FY26 (+3%) and fell 12% year on year in Q1FY27 as margins slipped and costs rose with spends. We forecast EPS of {{F.eps.0|n2}} / {{F.eps.1|n2}} / {{F.eps.2|n2}} for FY27-29E (growth {{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}}, {{F.epsGrowth.1|pct}}, {{F.epsGrowth.2|pct}}). All of FY27E's gain comes from lower loan losses: pre-provision profit is flat in our model ({{fin.ppop.11|num}} → {{F.ppop.0|num}} cr) and only starts growing again in FY28E as receivables pick up. ROE returns to ~17%, not to the 22-26% of FY22-FY24.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: real in distribution and parentage; weak in pricing and growth

blocks.p: A card issuer's moat shows up as cheap, low-risk customer acquisition, high activity per card and stable returns through a credit cycle. SBI Card scores well on the first, average on the second and poorly on the third: its ROE fell from 25.7% to 14.7% in two years. We test each source of advantage.

verdicts: Nearly half of new cards come through SBI (47% in Q1FY27); SBI has 53 crore customers, of whom management sees "at least 1.5-2 crore" as cardable; SBI also lends 45% of its borrowings.
Durable as long as SBI keeps the card business in-house; no other non-bank issuer has this.
18.6% of cards, 19.5% of spends; BPCL (5 million cards), Flipkart, Tata Neu, IndiGo, PhonePe, IRCTC, Apollo co-brands.
Scale brings network incentives and partner deals; co-brands can move between issuers when contracts end.
Credit cost 6.0% in FY23 but 9.1% in FY25 (our basis); stress in FY25-26 forced tighter limits and slower growth.
Not a shield: the book is unsecured and the customer base widened fast in FY22-24.
AAA/A1+, SBI lines, cost of funds 6.5%; but no deposits.
Cheaper than most NBFCs, dearer than bank issuers.
Revolvers fell from 24% to 22% as customers moved to personal loans; interchange take rate down from ~1.4% to 1.19%.
Card interest is exposed to cheaper credit; interchange to UPI and corporate mix.
App rated 4.5-4.6; 30-day active rate 52.5%; hyper-personalised offers; SPRINT digital onboarding.
NBFC rules (125% risk weight) but exempt from the NBFC revolving-credit draft; transactor relief possible.
Rules have cost it growth (BPSP, 2023 risk weights) more than they have helped.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** SBI Card has a narrow moat built on its parent: cheap, trusted acquisition through SBI and the scale that comes with it. It does not have pricing power, and its returns are not stable through a credit cycle. The moat protects its market share, not its margins.

sections.title: Q1FY27: profit +20% on credit cost; everything else was soft

blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026, reported 24-Jul-2026) had one strong number and several weak ones. Gross credit cost fell to 6.5% (7.7% in Q4, 9.5% a year earlier), so profit rose 20% to ₹664 cr and ROE reached 16.5%. But revenue from operations grew only 3%, receivables 3%, interest income fell 3%, NIM fell 28bp QoQ to 10.8%, operating cost rose 23% (spends, new cards, a wage-code provision) and cost-to-income rose to 58.7%. Earnings before credit cost fell 12% year on year. New accounts (+17%) and retail spends (+14%) were the leading indicators that improved.

blocks.callout: **Our read:** management guides on direction, not numbers, for growth and credit cost; the hard guidance (cost-to-income 56-58%, ROA 4-4.5% in the medium term) is consistent with our model. The one thing it has repeatedly promised and not yet delivered is receivables growth ("will lead to asset growth in the coming days", Apr-2026). Our FY27E needs that H2 pick-up; if it does not come, FY27E receivables growth would be ~4-5%; with spends unchanged that costs only ~1% of FY27E EPS and ~2% of FY28E, but it would undermine the case for a higher multiple.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books, but overlays and one-offs move quarters

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**, close to green. Joint auditors appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General (V. K. Dhingra & Co. and S. P. Chopra & Co.) gave an unmodified opinion on FY26; disclosure of asset quality (stages, write-offs, recoveries, ECL rates) is good. What a reader should watch:

bullets: **Overlays.** A ₹121 cr management overlay at Dec-2025 was raised to ₹220 cr at Mar-2026; in Q1FY27 ₹180 cr of it was used for the annual ECL model refresh, ₹65 cr of provisions were released on a better portfolio mix and ₹70 cr is still held. Without the release, Q1 credit cost would have been ~7.0%, not 6.5%.

**One-offs in Q4FY26.** Other income included ₹109 cr of liabilities and provisions written back in FY26 (mostly Q4: a GST liability write-back), and opex benefited from a payment-infrastructure fund (PIDF) reversal; management acknowledged "a couple of one-offs". Adjusted for them, Q4 cost-to-income was ~60%.

**Gross vs net credit cost.** Recoveries of written-off loans (₹686 cr in FY26) sit in other income; the company quotes both gross (8.6%) and net (7.4%) credit cost. We forecast both lines separately.

**Related parties.** SBI is lender (₹19,876 cr), distribution channel (₹177 cr of fees and commission paid) and brand owner (₹43 cr royalty). All stated at arm's length; the dependence is a strength and a governance consideration.

**Tax.** A ₹81 cr GST show-cause notice on input-tax credit (Jul-2025) and older service-tax and GST disputes on interchange income are disclosed as contingent liabilities; none was material to profit.

sections.title: A ₹66,000 crore balance sheet that is now over-capitalised: 4.2x assets to equity and falling

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 SBI Card had ₹66,328 cr of assets: ₹54,984 cr of card loans net of provisions (gross receivables ₹56,926 cr), ₹6,374 cr of investments (mostly government securities held for liquidity) and ₹2,320 cr of cash. It was funded by ₹15,726 cr of equity, ₹44,064 cr of borrowings and ₹6,539 cr of other liabilities (mostly payables to merchants and networks, and provisions). Equity capital has barely moved since FY20 (₹939 cr to ₹952 cr, employee options only): every rupee of equity growth since the 2020 listing has come from retained profit.

pair.title: Equity is growing faster than borrowings again
Cash flow turned positive in FY26 because the book stopped growing

blocks.callout: **Read this right:** a lender's operating cash flow is negative whenever its book grows, because new loans are an operating outflow. SBI Card's turned positive in FY26 (₹493 cr) for the wrong reason: receivables grew only 2%. With a 12% payout and receivables growing 8-13%, equity compounds faster than assets in our model, so leverage keeps falling ({{fin.assetsToEquity.11|n2}}x assets to equity in FY26 to {{fin.assetsToEquity.14|n2}}x in FY29E). That caps ROE unless growth returns or more cash is paid out.

sections.title: Ownership: State Bank of India controls 69%; domestic funds have replaced foreign ones

blocks.p: In Jun-2026 the promoter group held 68.86% (State Bank of India 68.58%). Domestic institutions held 18.13% (mutual funds 10.8%, insurers 6.56%, led by LIC with ~6.1%) and foreign investors 8.98%, down from 10.2% a year earlier. Retail holders own only 3.4%. ICICI Prudential's funds are the largest active holders (~6.4% across five schemes in the top 20) and added in the June quarter. The free float is small (~31%), which limits index weight and liquidity.

sections.title: Management and governance: a strong parent, a rotating CEO, and a board in flux

blocks.p: SBI Card is run as an SBI subsidiary. Its MD & CEO is an SBI officer on deputation: Salila Pande took over on 1-Apr-2025 for two years (previously CGM of SBI's Mumbai Metro Circle and CEO of SBI California), succeeding Abhijit Chakravorty; Ashwini Kumar Tewari, now SBI's MD for subsidiaries and a board member, ran the company in 2020. SBI's chairman (C. S. Setty) chairs the board. The professional team below the MD (CFO Rashmi Mohanty, CRO Krishna Kant Bishnoi, sales head Girish Budhiraja) provides continuity. The MD's pay was 16.6x the median employee's in FY26, modest by private-sector standards.

verdicts: 68.6% owner; lends 45% of borrowings; brand, branches and customer data; AAA rating rests on it.
The core of the investment case; also the main concentration risk.
Delivered the credit-cost turnaround it promised in FY26; growth promises ("asset growth in the coming days") not yet met.
Execution on risk is good; on growth, unproven.
CEOs rotate from SBI every two to three years; the current term runs to about Mar-2027 with no decision announced by 30-Sep-2026.
Strategy can shift with each CEO; long-term incentives are short.
Four independent directors left in 2025 (Jun, Aug, two in Nov); three joined (Apr, Nov, Dec-2025).
Unusual churn; we found no stated reason in the annual report.
Quarterly stage-wise asset quality, write-offs, recoveries, ECL rates, spends and mix.
No equity raised since the 2020 IPO; payout 11-12%; capital ratio 25.6% vs 15% required.
Conservative; surplus capital is not being returned.
SBI: ₹19,876 cr of loans, ₹1,357 cr of interest, ₹177 cr of fees and commission, ₹43.3 cr royalty (FY26).
Arm's length per the accounts; minority holders depend on that staying true.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** governance risk at SBI Card is not about honesty or accounting; it is about control. SBI decides who runs the company, for how long, how much capital it keeps and how much it pays out. That has kept the business safe and funded, but it also explains the low payout, the rotating leadership and the lack of a long-term equity incentive for management.

blocks.p: After Q1FY27 (24-Jul-2026) the street was divided. Motilal Oswal stayed Neutral with ₹700 (18x FY28E EPS: easing credit cost, but tepid growth and margin pressure); UBS cut to ₹700 (Neutral); Emkay kept Buy but cut to ₹750 (22x FY28E: "credit cost improves, but revenue growth challenges persist"); CLSA upgraded to Outperform, arguing slippage is well below normal; Jefferies stayed at Hold, saying stepped-up card additions should lift receivables "with lag, but pace is uncertain"; Bernstein stayed at Sell (₹430 per an aggregator, after ₹610 in April). P/E suits a card issuer because most of its income is fees and its book turns over every few months; book value says less about earning power than it does for a mortgage lender. We use the same method on the earnings the market will look at in September 2027 (Sep-28E: half FY28E, half FY29E), so our target is comparable. Targets are as they stood on 30-Sep-2026.

blocks.p: We start from the stock's own one-year-forward P/E since April 2021, as the house rule asks (no trough years: forward EPS never fell below half its prior peak). SBI Card's history needs one adjustment the rule does not make by itself: in FY25-FY26 credit costs of ~9% depressed EPS without collapsing it, so the forward P/E of those years looks inflated. We therefore also measure the history on EPS normalised to a 7.2% through-cycle credit cost, take the growth regime we forecast, apply the sector move, and convert back to our (below-normal credit cost) Sep-28E EPS. Peers, returns and the street are checks.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a BUY on the street's yardstick, resting on a re-rating the fundamentals do not guarantee

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's second-largest card issuer and its largest non-bank one: 2.26 crore cards, ~19% of national card spends, SBI's branches and balance sheet behind it, AAA funding, 25.6% capital, good disclosure, and a credit cycle that has just turned (gross credit cost 6.5% in Q1FY27 from 9.5% a year earlier). What you are not buying is growth: receivables grew 2% in FY26, revolvers are shrinking, and the take rate on spends is falling.

**What you are paying:** 19.4x FY27E and 16.0x FY28E EPS (the lowest forward P/E since listing); 3.0x FY27E book for a ~17% ROE. On the street's yardstick, and on its own credit-cycle-adjusted history (26.4x since Apr-2024 before the sector de-rating), that is cheap: 21x Sep-28E EPS gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) and a BUY. On fundamentals it is not: at a 13.1% cost of equity the price already implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} long-run ROE, and our justified P/B (₹468) and residual income (₹452) are below the price. The upside depends on growth returning and the market paying for it again.

bullets: **Rating: BUY, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.

**On today's numbers we would stay buyers below ~₹700 and turn sellers above ~₹850.** The rating is sensitive to the multiple: at 18x Sep-28E EPS (Motilal Oswal's multiple) the target is ~₹690 (still a BUY); at 16x (today's) ~₹620 (HOLD).
**Biggest swing factors:** credit cost (10bp ≈ 1.4% of FY28E EPS), receivables growth and the multiple (1x ≈ ₹39 a share).

**Portfolio fit:** a recovery position in Indian consumer credit with a strong parent, for investors who can wait for growth to return; size it for a bear case near {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}. It is not a compounder at today's ROE.

sections.title: Annotated financials (lender format)

blocks.p: Screener's NBFC layout, rebuilt into a lender income statement. Total income = interest income + fees and other operating income (interchange, fees, membership, network incentives); operating expenses include fees and commission paid and depreciation (the company's "operating cost"); provisions = impairment on financial instruments (write-offs plus the change in expected-loss provisions). Recoveries of written-off loans are in other income, so the company's "net credit cost" is provisions minus part of other income. Ratios use year-end averages, so they differ slightly from the company's monthly-average ratios.

sections.title: Glossary

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Non-banking financial company: a lender regulated by the RBI that cannot take current or savings deposits. SBI Card is a non-deposit-taking NBFC.
All cards issued and not cancelled, including suspended cards that can be reactivated.
The value of purchases made with the cards (retail = individuals; corporate = company cards).

What cardholders owe at a date: the lender's "AUM". Transactors pay in full each month (no interest); revolvers carry a balance and pay interest; EMI balances are purchases converted into instalments.
The fee the merchant's bank pays the card issuer on each purchase; take rate = interchange ÷ spends.
New cards sourced through SBI's branches and app / through co-brand partners and direct sales.
A card issued with a partner (e.g. BPCL, Flipkart) that offers rewards on that partner's spending.
Net interest income = interest earned − interest paid. Net interest margin = NII ÷ average receivables.
Write-offs plus the change in loss provisions ÷ average receivables; net = after recoveries of loans already written off.
Ind AS 109 buckets: performing, 30-89 days overdue (and other higher-risk accounts), 90-179 days overdue. ECL = expected credit loss provisions held against them.
Gross / net Stage 3 loans as % of receivables; provision coverage = provisions on Stage 3 ÷ Stage 3 loans.
An extra provision booked on management's judgement on top of the model-based ECL.
Operating cost ÷ net revenue. Company basis includes other income (recoveries) in revenue; our basis uses NII + fees only.
Capital ÷ risk-weighted assets (minimum 15% for NBFCs; Tier 1 at least 10%). The risk weight is the share of a loan counted for capital: 125% for NBFC card receivables since Nov-2023.
Profit ÷ average total assets; profit ÷ average shareholders' equity.
Price ÷ EPS; price ÷ book value per share. Justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (cost of equity − g).
Book value plus the present value of future profit above the cost of equity.
EPS recalculated as if gross credit cost had been at the through-cycle level (7.2%), used to read the stock's P/E history.
Half FY28E plus half FY29E: the earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
Business payment solution providers (routing company payments through cards); the RBI's Payments Infrastructure Development Fund; RuPay credit cards linked to UPI for QR payments.
